title: Yellow Eyes After Drinking: Causes and When to See a Doctor
excerpt: Yellow eyes after drinking aren't a normal hangover. What turns the eyes yellow, from harmless Gilbert's syndrome to alcohol-related hepatitis, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Yellow eyes after drinking aren't a hangover. Learn the causes, from harmless Gilbert's syndrome to liver disease, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
> **When to see a doctor.** Yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice) is never a normal hangover symptom. **See a doctor within 24 hours** for any new yellow tint to the whites of your eyes, even if you feel fine. **Get same-day emergency care (call 911 in the US)** if yellow eyes come with confusion, drowsiness, or personality changes; vomiting blood or coffee-ground material; black, tarry, or bloody stools; a rapidly swelling belly; fever with right-sided belly pain; severe upper belly pain that spreads to your back; or easy bruising and bleeding. If you drink heavily every day and get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, tell your doctor before cutting back, because stopping suddenly can trigger dangerous withdrawal. This article is general information, not medical advice.

**The honest answer first:** a normal night of drinking should not turn the whites of your eyes yellow. Red, bloodshot, or tired-looking eyes after drinking are common and harmless. A true yellow tint is different. It means a pigment called bilirubin is building up in your blood, and that usually points to something going on with your liver, your bile ducts, or your red blood cells. Sometimes the cause is mild and harmless, like a common inherited quirk called Gilbert's syndrome that flares up when you're dehydrated and haven't eaten. Sometimes it's serious, like alcohol-related hepatitis. You can't tell which from the mirror, so treat yellow eyes after drinking as a warning sign and call a doctor today.

**The quick rules:** If the whites of your eyes look yellow, book a doctor's appointment within 24 hours and ask for a liver blood test. Go to urgent care or the emergency room the same day if the yellow comes with confusion or unusual sleepiness, a swollen belly, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, a fever with pain under your right ribs, or severe stomach pain that spreads to your back. Stop drinking until you've been checked. If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly on your own; talk to a doctor first, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

## Why Eyes Turn Yellow: Bilirubin in Plain Words

Your body is constantly replacing old red blood cells. When an old one breaks down, the hemoglobin inside it is turned into a yellow-orange pigment called **bilirubin**. That bilirubin travels through your blood to your liver, where it gets chemically packaged (doctors call this "conjugation") so it can dissolve in bile. The bile drains through small ducts into your gut, and the bilirubin eventually leaves your body in your stool. That's actually what gives stool its brown color.

Yellowing happens when bilirubin builds up faster than your body can clear it. The extra pigment seeps into tissues, and the whites of the eyes are usually the first place it shows because they're pale and contain a lot of elastic tissue that binds bilirubin. Doctors call yellow eyes **scleral icterus**, and yellow skin and eyes together **jaundice**. The eyes typically start looking yellow when blood bilirubin climbs to roughly two to three times the upper end of normal, which is why yellow eyes often show up before yellow skin.

There are three broad places this process can go wrong:

1. **Before the liver (too much bilirubin made).** If red blood cells break down faster than usual, the liver gets more bilirubin than it can handle. This is less often linked to alcohol.
2. **Inside the liver (the liver can't process it).** Inflammation or scarring of the liver, or an inherited slowness in the packaging step, means bilirubin backs up in the blood. Most alcohol-related causes live here.
3. **After the liver (the drain is blocked).** A gallstone, a swollen pancreas, or, rarely, a tumor can squeeze or block the bile ducts so bile can't drain out. Bilirubin backs up into the blood instead.

Alcohol can be involved in all three, but the most common alcohol-related reasons for yellow eyes are in the middle group. Here's how they line up.

## Can One Night of Drinking Cause Yellow Eyes?

In a healthy liver, a single night of drinking, even a heavy one, should not cause jaundice. Your liver has a lot of spare capacity. A binge can stress it and briefly raise some liver enzymes, but visible yellowing from one night out in someone with a healthy liver would be unusual.

There are a few situations where yellow eyes can show up right after a night or a weekend of drinking:

- **You have Gilbert's syndrome and didn't know it.** This is the most common harmless explanation, and it's covered in detail below. The yellow tends to appear after a combination of drinking, not eating, poor sleep, and dehydration, and fades within a few days.
- **The drinking was part of a longer heavy pattern.** Alcohol-related hepatitis often surfaces after a stretch of heavier-than-usual drinking in someone who has been drinking heavily for months or years. To the person, it can feel like "I went on a bender and then my eyes went yellow," but the groundwork was laid long before.
- **The binge triggered something else.** Heavy drinking is one of the two leading causes of acute pancreatitis (gallstones are the other), and a swollen pancreas can squeeze the bile duct. A gallstone can also move and block the duct around the same time. Both usually cause significant belly pain, not just yellow eyes.
- **You also took acetaminophen.** Taking a lot of Tylenol, or Tylenol in several products, on top of heavy drinking can injure the liver. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why and how much is too much.

So for a one-off night, it's not "just a hangover," but it's also not automatically a disaster. It needs a blood test to sort out.

## Gilbert's Syndrome: The Common, Harmless Reason Some People Go Yellow After Drinking

Gilbert's syndrome is an inherited condition where the liver is a little slow at packaging bilirubin, because a gene that makes the packaging enzyme (called UGT1A1) works at reduced capacity. It's common. Estimates usually put it at somewhere around 3 to 7 percent of people, and many of them never find out they have it. It's harmless: it doesn't damage the liver, doesn't progress to liver disease, and doesn't need treatment.

Most of the time people with Gilbert's have normal or slightly raised bilirubin and no symptoms. But bilirubin can rise enough to make the eyes look faintly yellow when the body is under certain kinds of stress. The well-known triggers include:

- **Fasting or skipping meals**, which is one of the most reliable triggers
- **Dehydration**
- **Illness**, like a cold, the flu, or a stomach bug
- **Lack of sleep and physical or emotional stress**
- **Hard exercise**
- **Menstruation**, in some people
- **Alcohol**, which many people with Gilbert's notice makes it worse

Look at that list and then think about a typical big night out: drinks, not much food, a late night, poor sleep, dehydration, maybe vomiting. It hits almost every trigger at once. That's why someone with Gilbert's might first notice yellow eyes the morning after a party, or after a festival weekend, and then see it fade a few days later once they're eating, sleeping, and drinking water again.

Some people with Gilbert's also say they feel worse after drinking than their friends do, with more fatigue or nausea. Research hasn't clearly settled whether Gilbert's causes these symptoms or whether people just notice them more, so treat that as an open question.

**The important part:** you can't diagnose yourself with Gilbert's. It's a diagnosis doctors make after ruling out other causes. Typically your blood tests show a raised level of the "unconjugated" (unpackaged) type of bilirubin, while your liver enzymes and blood counts are normal. If that's your pattern, a doctor may be confident it's Gilbert's. Until you've been checked, assume yellow eyes need looking at.

If you do have Gilbert's, the practical advice is simple: eat regular meals, especially around drinking, stay hydrated, get sleep, and expect that heavy drinking nights may bring a faint yellow tint back.

## Alcohol-Related Liver Disease: When Yellow Eyes Are a Warning

The more serious reasons for yellow eyes after drinking come from damage to the liver itself. Doctors usually describe alcohol-related liver disease in three overlapping stages.

### Alcohol-related fatty liver

This is the earliest stage and by far the most common. Fat builds up in liver cells after a period of heavy drinking. It usually causes no symptoms at all and does **not** typically cause yellow eyes. It's mostly found on blood tests or scans done for other reasons. The good news is that it can reverse, often within weeks to a few months of stopping or greatly cutting back on alcohol. Our [fatty liver disease guide](/never-hungover/fatty-liver-disease-complete-guide-causes-symptoms-natural-treatment-2025) covers it in more depth.

### Alcohol-related hepatitis

This is inflammation of the liver caused by alcohol, and jaundice is its hallmark symptom. It usually affects people who have been drinking heavily for a long time, but it can come on fairly suddenly, often after a stretch of heavier drinking. Symptoms can include:

- Yellow eyes and skin that come on over days to weeks
- Loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting
- Pain or tenderness under the right ribs
- Low-grade fever
- Tiredness and weakness
- A swollen belly from fluid buildup
- In severe cases, confusion

Severe alcohol-related hepatitis is a medical emergency that can be life-threatening, and it is treated in hospital. Milder cases can improve a great deal if the person stops drinking. The single most important treatment at every level of severity is stopping alcohol.

### Cirrhosis

Cirrhosis is advanced scarring of the liver after years of damage. Many people with early cirrhosis feel fine. As it progresses, the liver loses the ability to do its jobs, and jaundice can appear along with fluid in the belly, swelling in the legs, easy bruising, spider-like blood vessels on the skin, red palms, itching, and confusion. Cirrhosis can't be fully undone, but stopping drinking can slow or stop it from getting worse and greatly improves outcomes.

### How much drinking are we talking about?

There's no single number that guarantees liver disease or rules it out. Genes, body size, sex, weight, other liver conditions like hepatitis B or C, and diet all change the risk. Women tend to develop alcohol-related liver damage at lower levels of drinking than men. In general, the risk of serious liver disease climbs with heavy drinking over many years. If you drink above the limits in your country's guidelines most weeks and you've noticed yellow eyes, take it seriously and get checked promptly rather than waiting to see if it goes away.

## Other Things That Can Cause Yellow Eyes Around Drinking

Not every yellow eye after a night out is about alcohol and the liver directly.

**Gallstones.** A gallstone can slip out of the gallbladder and block the main bile duct. This typically causes yellow eyes along with pain in the upper right belly, and sometimes fever and chills if the duct gets infected. A fatty meal, like a late-night or hangover fry-up, can set off gallbladder pain. Fever plus jaundice plus right-sided pain needs same-day care.

**Pancreatitis.** Heavy drinking is a major cause of acute pancreatitis, a painful inflammation of the pancreas. The classic symptom is severe pain in the upper belly that often spreads to the back, usually with nausea and vomiting. Swelling can press on the bile duct and cause yellow eyes. This needs emergency care.

**Viral hepatitis.** Hepatitis A, B, C, and E infect the liver and can cause jaundice. They have nothing to do with drinking, but alcohol makes the liver damage from hepatitis B and C worse. It's worth remembering that yellow eyes after a trip, a festival, or a new sexual partner might be an infection rather than the drinks.

**Medicines and supplements.** Acetaminophen in large or repeated doses, some antibiotics, and a range of herbal and bodybuilding supplements can injure the liver. Tell your doctor about everything you've taken, including supplements.

**Red blood cell breakdown.** Some inherited conditions, such as G6PD deficiency, and some infections and medicines can make red blood cells break down faster, raising bilirubin. This is less commonly tied to alcohol.

### Things that look yellow but aren't jaundice

Before you worry, make sure it's really yellowing:

- **Pinguecula.** A small, raised, yellowish patch on the white of the eye, usually on the side nearest the nose. It's a harmless growth linked to sun, wind, and dust exposure. Jaundice colors the whole white of the eye evenly; a pinguecula is a spot.
- **Natural tint with age.** Some older adults have a slight yellowish or brownish tinge to the whites of their eyes from normal changes in the tissue, and people with darker skin often have some natural pigment there. If you've always looked this way, it's probably your normal.
- **Too much beta-carotene.** Eating a lot of carrots, sweet potatoes, or squash can turn the skin, especially the palms, orange-yellow. This is called carotenemia and it's harmless. The key difference: **it doesn't turn the whites of your eyes yellow.** If your eyes are clearly yellow, carotene isn't the explanation.
- **Lighting.** Warm bathroom bulbs make everything look yellow. Check your eyes in daylight, next to a window, and pull down your lower lid to look at the white below the colored part.

For the more common red, irritated, or dry eyes after drinking, see our guide to [alcohol and eye health](/never-hungover/alcohol-eye-health-complete-vision-impact-guide-2025).

## Symptoms to Check Alongside Yellow Eyes

When you talk to a doctor, these details help them narrow it down quickly. Take a moment to notice whether you have any of them:

| Symptom | What it can suggest |
|---|---|
| Dark urine, like tea or cola, even when you're drinking water | Bilirubin is spilling into the urine, which happens with liver or bile duct problems (not with Gilbert's) |
| Pale, clay-colored, or grey stools | Bile isn't reaching the gut, which can mean a blocked duct |
| Itchy skin, especially palms and soles | Bile salts building up in the blood; see our guide to [itchy skin after drinking](/never-hungover/itchy-skin-after-drinking) for the more common causes |
| Pain or ache under the right ribs | Liver inflammation, or gallbladder and bile duct trouble; our [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) guide explains this area |
| Severe upper belly pain spreading to the back | Possible pancreatitis; get emergency care |
| Fever or chills | Possible infection of the bile ducts or liver; get same-day care |
| Swollen belly or swollen ankles | Fluid buildup, which can happen with advanced liver disease |
| Confusion, sleepiness, or acting "off" | The liver may not be clearing toxins; this is an emergency |
| Vomiting blood or black stools | Possible bleeding in the gut; this is an emergency (see [vomiting blood after drinking](/never-hungover/vomiting-blood-after-drinking)) |
| Yellow eyes only, feeling otherwise fine, fades in a few days | Fits Gilbert's syndrome, but still needs a blood test to confirm |

## What the Doctor Will Check

You don't need to prepare much. Be honest about how much and how often you drink, because it really does change what the doctor looks for, and they've heard it all before. Bring a list of every medicine and supplement you've taken in the past few weeks, including how much acetaminophen.

Common first steps include:

- **Bilirubin tests.** These measure total bilirubin and split it into "unconjugated" (not yet processed by the liver) and "conjugated" (processed). A high unconjugated level with otherwise normal results points toward Gilbert's or red blood cell breakdown. A high conjugated level points toward the liver or the bile ducts.
- **A liver panel.** This includes enzymes called ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT. The pattern matters. In alcohol-related liver injury, AST is often noticeably higher than ALT, and GGT is often raised by regular drinking.
- **A complete blood count.** This checks for anemia and signs of red blood cell breakdown, and the platelet count can hint at liver scarring.
- **Clotting tests (INR) and albumin.** These show how well the liver is doing its manufacturing jobs.
- **Viral hepatitis tests**, when appropriate.
- **An abdominal ultrasound.** A quick, painless scan that looks for fatty liver, scarring, gallstones, and blocked or widened bile ducts.

Depending on the results, you might be sent for more scans, a specialized scan that measures liver stiffness, or a referral to a liver specialist.

## What to Do Right Now

If you've just noticed yellow eyes after drinking and you don't have any of the emergency signs listed above:

1. **Stop drinking until you've been checked.** Whatever the cause, alcohol won't help, and if it's liver inflammation, more alcohol makes it worse.
2. **Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol) unless a doctor says it's okay**, and check cold, flu, and sleep products for it. Don't start new herbal supplements or "detox" products either.
3. **Eat regular meals and drink water.** If it turns out to be Gilbert's, this alone often helps the yellow fade.
4. **Book a doctor's appointment within 24 hours** and ask for a liver blood test.
5. **Watch for the emergency signs** and go to the emergency room if any appear.

**A note for daily heavy drinkers.** If you drink a lot every day and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you go without, stopping suddenly can cause alcohol withdrawal, which can include seizures and can be dangerous. That isn't a reason to keep drinking. It's a reason to tell a doctor today so they can help you stop safely, sometimes with medicine.

## How Long Do Yellow Eyes Last After Drinking?

It depends entirely on the cause:

- **Gilbert's syndrome:** the yellow usually fades within a few days once you're eating, hydrating, and resting again.
- **Alcohol-related hepatitis:** jaundice can take weeks to months to clear after stopping drinking, and it may get worse before it gets better.
- **Gallstones or a blocked duct:** jaundice usually clears once the blockage is removed, often with a procedure.
- **Cirrhosis:** jaundice may come and go and can signal that the liver is struggling, which needs ongoing specialist care.

If yellow eyes linger more than a few days, keep coming back, or get deeper in color, that's another reason to get checked promptly.

## Is It Reversible?

Often, yes, especially when it's caught early:

- Gilbert's isn't a disease to reverse. It's lifelong and harmless.
- Alcohol-related fatty liver usually reverses with stopping or greatly cutting back.
- Mild to moderate alcohol-related hepatitis can improve substantially if drinking stops, though recovery takes time.
- Cirrhosis scarring generally can't be fully undone, but stopping alcohol can halt further damage and significantly improve health and life expectancy.

The liver is remarkably good at healing when given the chance. The earlier you find out what's going on, the more options you have.

## Can Supplements Help?

Be wary of anything sold as a quick fix for yellow eyes. There is no good evidence that any supplement treats jaundice, and some "liver detox" products have themselves been linked to liver injury. If your eyes are yellow, a supplement is not a substitute for a blood test. That includes hangover supplements: we don't recommend any product on this page, because the next step for yellow eyes is a blood test, not a purchase. If you also have pain under your right ribs, our guide to [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) explains what it can mean.

Once a doctor has checked you and says your liver is healthy, and only then, the habits with the best evidence are the plain ones: drink less, drink slower, eat before and while drinking, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through them.

## The Bottom Line

Yellow eyes are not a hangover symptom. They mean bilirubin is building up, and the cause can range from harmless Gilbert's syndrome, which often shows up after a night of drinking, skipping meals, and poor sleep, to serious alcohol-related hepatitis, gallstones, or pancreatitis. You can't tell which by looking. Stop drinking for now, avoid Tylenol, eat and hydrate, and see a doctor within 24 hours for a simple blood test. Go to the emergency room straight away if yellow eyes come with confusion, vomiting blood, black stools, a swollen belly, fever with right-sided pain, or severe belly pain.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can drinking alcohol cause yellow eyes?**

Yes, but not usually from a normal night out. Yellow eyes mean bilirubin is building up in your blood. Alcohol-related causes include alcohol-related hepatitis and cirrhosis after long-term heavy drinking, pancreatitis or gallstones that block the bile duct, and flare-ups of Gilbert's syndrome, a harmless inherited condition. Any new yellowing of the eyes should be checked by a doctor with a blood test.

**Can one night of drinking cause yellow eyes?**

In someone with a healthy liver, a single night of drinking shouldn't cause visible jaundice. If your eyes look yellow after one night, the most common harmless explanation is Gilbert's syndrome, which flares with drinking, fasting, dehydration, and poor sleep. Less often, a binge can trigger pancreatitis or reveal liver inflammation that built up over a longer period. A doctor's visit and a liver blood test will tell you which.

**What is Gilbert's syndrome and why does it make my eyes yellow after drinking?**

Gilbert's syndrome is a common inherited condition where the liver processes bilirubin a bit more slowly than usual. It's harmless and doesn't damage the liver. Bilirubin can rise enough to tint the eyes when you skip meals, get dehydrated, sleep badly, get sick, or drink, which is why a big night out can bring it on. The yellow usually fades in a few days. Only a doctor can confirm it, after ruling out other causes.

**Is jaundice after drinking an emergency?**

New jaundice needs a doctor within 24 hours even if you feel fine. It becomes an emergency if it comes with confusion or drowsiness, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black or tarry stools, a swollen belly, fever with pain under the right ribs, or severe upper belly pain spreading to the back. In those cases, go to the emergency room or call 911 in the US.

**How long do yellow eyes last after drinking?**

It depends on the cause. With Gilbert's syndrome, the yellow usually fades within a few days of eating, hydrating, and resting. With alcohol-related hepatitis, it can take weeks to months after stopping alcohol. If it's caused by a gallstone, it usually clears once the blockage is treated. Yellow that lasts more than a few days, keeps returning, or deepens needs prompt medical attention.

**Are yellow eyes from alcohol reversible?**

Often, yes, if the cause is found early. Gilbert's is harmless and lifelong. Alcohol-related fatty liver usually reverses after stopping or cutting back on drinking, and alcohol-related hepatitis can improve a lot if drinking stops. Cirrhosis scarring generally can't be fully undone, but stopping alcohol can prevent further damage and greatly improve outcomes.

**What do dark urine and yellow eyes together mean?**

Dark, tea-colored urine alongside yellow eyes suggests the processed type of bilirubin is spilling into the urine, which happens with liver inflammation or a blocked bile duct. It isn't typical of Gilbert's syndrome. Pale or clay-colored stools at the same time point more strongly toward a blockage. This combination needs a doctor promptly, the same day if you also have pain or fever.

**Should I stop drinking if my eyes are yellow?**

Yes. Stop drinking until a doctor has checked you, and avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) unless they say it's okay. If you drink heavily every day and feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you go without, don't stop suddenly on your own. Tell a doctor right away, because alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous and they can help you stop safely.

**Can DHM or liver supplements fix yellow eyes?**

No. There is no good evidence that any supplement treats jaundice, and some liver detox products have been linked to liver injury themselves. DHM has early research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly in animals, but it is not a treatment for liver disease. If your eyes are yellow, see a doctor first and ask before taking any supplement.
